021-substitution-into-expressions.title:
ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS,
(SUBSTITUTION INTO EXPRESSIONS)
021-substitution-into-expressions.objective: LO: I can substitute given values into algebraic expressions and evaluate the result.

content.text: Substitution means replacing a letter with a given number, then working out the value of the expression.
Remember: 2x means 2 × x. When we write letters next to numbers or other letters, multiplication is implied.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Replace the letter with the number. Use BIDMAS to work out the answer in the correct order.
key_idea.caption: Substitute then calculate

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – single variable
modelled_examples.question: Find the value of 4x + 3 when x = 5
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply first (BIDMAS), then add.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – two variables
modelled_examples.question: Find the value of 3a + 2b when a = 4 and b = 5
steps: Replace a with 4 and b with 5: 3 × 4 + 2 × 5
modelled_examples.explanation: Substitute both letters, then follow BIDMAS.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – with powers
modelled_examples.question: Find the value of x² + 3x when x = 4
modelled_examples.explanation: Powers first, then multiplication, then addition.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – negative values
modelled_examples.question: Find the value of 2x² − 3x when x = −2
modelled_examples.explanation: (−2)² = 4, not −4. A negative squared gives a positive.

022-using-and-writing-simple-formulae.title:
ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS,
(USING AND WRITING SIMPLE FORMULAE)
022-using-and-writing-simple-formulae.objective: LO: I can write and use simple algebraic formulae to solve problems.

content.text: A formula is a mathematical rule written with letters and numbers that shows the relationship between quantities.
Remember: The subject of a formula is the single letter on its own, usually on the left side of the equals sign.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Identify the variables, write the rule using letters, then substitute values to evaluate.
key_idea.caption: 5 per item plus 10 fixed cost

modelled_examples.explanation: Identify the fixed part and the variable part.

023-expanding-double-brackets.title:
ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS,
(EXPANDING DOUBLE BRACKETS)
023-expanding-double-brackets.objective: LO: I can expand the product of two binomials using the FOIL method or grid method.

key_terms.title: What does expanding double brackets mean?

content.text: Expanding double brackets means multiplying two expressions like (x + 3)(x + 5) to remove the brackets and write as a single expression.
FOIL: First, Outside, Inside, Last. Multiply each pair then collect like terms.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket, then simplify by collecting like terms.
key_idea.equation: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab
key_idea.caption: Middle term = sum, last term = product

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – both positive
modelled_examples.question: Expand (x + 2)(x + 5)
steps: F: x × x = x², O: x × 5 = 5x, I: 2 × x = 2x, L: 2 × 5 = 10
modelled_examples.explanation: Collect the two middle terms: 5x + 2x = 7x.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – one negative
modelled_examples.question: Expand (x + 4)(x − 3)
modelled_examples.explanation: Be careful with signs: +4 × −3 = −12.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – both negative
modelled_examples.question: Expand (x − 3)(x − 4)
modelled_examples.explanation: Negative × negative = positive for the last term.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – perfect square
modelled_examples.question: Expand (x + 5)²
modelled_examples.explanation: A perfect square always gives x² + 2ax + a².

practice.heading: One negative term
practice.instruction: Expand and simplify. Watch the signs!

024-expanding-single-brackets.title:
ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS,
(EXPANDING SINGLE BRACKETS)
024-expanding-single-brackets.objective: LO: I can expand single brackets by multiplying every term inside by the term outside.

content.text: Expanding means removing the brackets by multiplying every term inside by the term outside.
Common error: only multiplying the first term. You must multiply BOTH terms inside the bracket.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply the term outside by EVERY term inside. Watch the signs carefully when there's a negative outside.
key_idea.caption: Multiply both terms

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – all positive
modelled_examples.question: Expand 3(x + 4)
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply each term inside by 3.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – with subtraction
modelled_examples.question: Expand 5(x − 2)
modelled_examples.explanation: The minus sign belongs to the 2.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – negative outside
modelled_examples.question: Expand −2(x + 3)
modelled_examples.explanation: Negative × positive = negative.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – variable outside
modelled_examples.question: Expand x(x + 5)
modelled_examples.explanation: x times x is x squared.

025-factorising-expressions.title:
ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS,
(FACTORISING EXPRESSIONS)
025-factorising-expressions.objective: LO: I can factorise algebraic expressions by taking out common factors.

content.text: Factorising is the reverse of expanding. We find a common factor and write the expression as a product of terms.
Strategy: Find the HCF of all terms (both numbers and letters), then divide each term by it.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of all terms. Write it outside the bracket. Divide each term by the HCF to get what goes inside.
key_idea.caption: HCF = 4x; divide each term by 4x

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – number HCF
modelled_examples.question: Factorise 6x + 9
modelled_examples.explanation: Check by expanding: 3 × 2x + 3 × 3 = 6x + 9 ✓

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – letter HCF
modelled_examples.question: Factorise x² + 5x
modelled_examples.explanation: Take out the lowest power of x from each term.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – number and letter
modelled_examples.question: Factorise 4x² + 8x
steps: HCF of 4 and 8 is 4; both have x: HCF = 4x
modelled_examples.explanation: Always take the highest common factor, including letters.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – three terms
modelled_examples.question: Factorise 6x² + 12x + 18
modelled_examples.explanation: When all coefficients share a common factor, take it out.

practice.heading: Letter common factor
practice.instruction: Take out the highest power of the letter.

026-angles-in-parallel-lines.title:
ANGLES AND GEOMETRY,
(ANGLES IN PARALLEL LINES)
026-angles-in-parallel-lines.objective: LO: I can identify and calculate alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles in parallel lines.

content.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, special angle pairs are formed: alternate, corresponding, and co-interior angles.
Remember: Alternate angles are equal (Z-shape). Corresponding angles are equal (F-shape). Co-interior angles add up to 180°.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Look for the Z, F, or C/U shape to identify the angle relationship. Then use equal or sum to 180°.
key_idea.caption: Z = equal, F = equal, C = 180°

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – alternate angles
modelled_examples.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is 65°. Find the alternate angle.
modelled_examples.explanation: Alternate angles are always equal when lines are parallel.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – corresponding angles

modelled_examples.explanation: Corresponding angles are in the same position at each intersection.

modelled_examples.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 72°. Find the other.
modelled_examples.explanation: Co-interior (allied) angles always add up to 180°.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – finding unknown
modelled_examples.question: In parallel lines, angle x and 3x are co-interior. Find x.
modelled_examples.explanation: Form an equation using the angle fact, then solve.

027-angles-in-polygons.title:
ANGLES AND GEOMETRY,
(ANGLES IN POLYGONS)
027-angles-in-polygons.objective: LO: I can find interior and exterior angles of regular and irregular polygons.

content.text: The sum of interior angles of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°.
Exterior angles: The exterior angles of any convex polygon always sum to 360°. Each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360° ÷ n.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles always sum to 360°.
key_idea.caption: n = number of sides

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – interior angle sum
modelled_examples.question: Find the sum of interior angles of a hexagon.
steps: A hexagon has 6 sides, so n = 6
modelled_examples.explanation: Always subtract 2 from the number of sides first.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – one interior angle (regular)

modelled_examples.explanation: For regular polygons, divide the total by the number of sides.

modelled_examples.question: Find one exterior angle of a regular pentagon.
modelled_examples.explanation: Exterior angle + interior angle = 180° (check: 108 + 72 = 180).

modelled_examples.explanation: Subtract the known angles from the total angle sum.

ANGLES AND GEOMETRY,

028-angles-in-triangles-and-quadrilatera.objective: LO: I can find missing angles in triangles and quadrilaterals using angle sum facts.

content.text: The angles in a triangle always add up to 180°. The angles in a quadrilateral always add up to 360°.
Types of triangle: Equilateral (all 60°), isosceles (two equal), scalene (all different), right-angled (one 90°).

029-angles-on-a-straight-line-and-at-a-p.title:
ANGLES AND GEOMETRY,

029-angles-on-a-straight-line-and-at-a-p.objective: LO: I can use the facts that angles on a straight line sum to 180° and angles at a point sum to 360°.

content.text: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°.
Vertically opposite: When two lines cross, the opposite angles are equal.

examples.expr: Angles on a line sum to 360°

key_idea.text: Straight line = 180°. Full turn = 360°. Vertically opposite = equal.
key_idea.equation: a + b = 180° (on a line); a + b + c + d = 360° (at a point)
key_idea.caption: Two fundamental angle facts

030-area-of-rectangles-triangles-and-par.title:
AREA AND PERIMETER,
(AREA OF RECTANGLES, TRIANGLES AND PARALLELOGRAMS)
030-area-of-rectangles-triangles-and-par.objective: LO: I can calculate the area of rectangles, triangles and parallelograms.

content.text: Area is the amount of space inside a 2D shape, measured in square units (cm², m²).
Formulae: Rectangle: A = l × w. Triangle: A = &frac{1}{2} × b × h. Parallelogram: A = b × h (perpendicular height).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Always use the PERPENDICULAR height (not the slant). Triangle is half of the enclosing rectangle.
key_idea.caption: Triangle: half base times height

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – rectangle
modelled_examples.question: Find the area of a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm.
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply length by width.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – triangle
modelled_examples.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.
modelled_examples.explanation: Half of base times height.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – parallelogram
modelled_examples.question: A parallelogram has base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. Find its area.
modelled_examples.explanation: Use the perpendicular height, not the slant side.

modelled_examples.question: A triangle has area 24 cm² and base 8 cm. Find the height.
modelled_examples.explanation: Rearrange the formula: h = 2A ÷ b.

032-circumference-of-a-circle.title:
AREA AND PERIMETER,
(CIRCUMFERENCE OF A CIRCLE)
032-circumference-of-a-circle.objective: LO: I can calculate the circumference of a circle using C = πd or C = 2πr.

content.text: The circumference is the distance around a circle. The diameter goes across through the centre; the radius is half the diameter.
Formulae: C = πd or C = 2πr (same thing because d = 2r). Use π = 3.14159... or the π button on a calculator.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Circumference = π × diameter. If given the radius, double it first (or use C = 2πr).
key_idea.caption: π is approximately 3.14

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – given diameter

modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply π by the diameter.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – given radius

modelled_examples.explanation: Double the radius to get the diameter, then multiply by π.

modelled_examples.explanation: Rearrange: divide circumference by π.

modelled_examples.explanation: Semicircle perimeter = half circumference + diameter.

039-comparing-fractions-decimals-and-per.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES,
(COMPARING FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES)
039-comparing-fractions-decimals-and-per.objective: LO: I can convert between fractions, decimals and percentages and compare their values.

content.text: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways to express the same value. Convert to the same form to compare.
Key conversions: Fraction → decimal: divide top by bottom. Decimal → %: multiply by 100. % → fraction: put over 100 and simplify.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: To compare, convert all values to the same form (usually decimals or percentages).
key_idea.caption: Divide then multiply to convert right

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – fraction to decimal
modelled_examples.question: Convert &frac{3}{8} to a decimal.
modelled_examples.explanation: Fraction means numerator divided by denominator.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – decimal to percentage
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.45 to a percentage.
modelled_examples.explanation: Move the decimal point two places right.

040-finding-percentages-of-amounts.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES,
(FINDING PERCENTAGES OF AMOUNTS)
040-finding-percentages-of-amounts.objective: LO: I can calculate a percentage of a given amount using mental and written methods.

content.text: Finding a percentage of an amount means finding that fraction of the total. 'Of' means multiply.
Method: Divide by 100, then multiply by the percentage. Or find 10% first and build up.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: To find x% of an amount: divide by 100, multiply by x. Or use 10% building blocks.
key_idea.caption: Percentage means per hundred

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simple percentage
modelled_examples.question: Find 20% of £150.
modelled_examples.explanation: Find 10% first, then double it.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – using division
modelled_examples.question: Find 35% of 200.
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide by 100 to get 1%, then multiply.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – non-calculator
modelled_examples.question: Find 15% of £80.
modelled_examples.explanation: Build up from 10% and 5%.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – applied
modelled_examples.question: A coat costs £120. There is a 30% discount. How much is the discount?
modelled_examples.explanation: The discount means you save £36; sale price = £84.

practice.instruction: Find each percentage of the amount.

041-percentage-increase-and-decrease.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES,
(PERCENTAGE INCREASE AND DECREASE)
041-percentage-increase-and-decrease.objective: LO: I can increase or decrease an amount by a given percentage.

content.text: A percentage increase means adding that percentage of the original. A percentage decrease means subtracting it.
Multiplier method: Increase by 20% → multiply by 1.20. Decrease by 15% → multiply by 0.85.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Increase: multiply by (1 + rate). Decrease: multiply by (1 − rate).
key_idea.caption: Multiplier = 1 ± percentage as decimal

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – percentage increase
modelled_examples.question: Increase £250 by 20%.
modelled_examples.explanation: Add the percentage to the original.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – percentage decrease
modelled_examples.question: Decrease £180 by 15%.
modelled_examples.explanation: Subtract the percentage from the original.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – multiplier method
modelled_examples.question: A house worth £200,000 increases by 5%. Find new value.
modelled_examples.explanation: The multiplier method does it in one step.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – sale price
modelled_examples.question: A jacket costs £85. It is reduced by 40% in a sale. Find the sale price.
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply by 0.60 because you pay 60% of the original.

practice.instruction: Increase each amount by the given percentage.

practice.heading: Percentage decrease
practice.instruction: Decrease each amount by the given percentage.

042-percentages-as-fractions-and-decimal.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES,
(PERCENTAGES AS FRACTIONS AND DECIMALS)
042-percentages-as-fractions-and-decimal.objective: LO: I can convert between percentages, fractions and decimals fluently.

key_terms.title: Three forms of the same value

content.text: Every percentage can be written as a fraction (over 100, then simplify) or a decimal (divide by 100).
Tip: Learn key equivalents: &frac{1}{2} = 50% = 0.5, &frac{1}{4} = 25% = 0.25, &frac{1}{5} = 20% = 0.2, &frac{1}{10} = 10% = 0.1.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: % to fraction: put over 100, simplify. % to decimal: divide by 100. Reverse to go back.
key_idea.caption: Percentage means per hundred

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – percentage to fraction
modelled_examples.question: Convert 60% to a fraction in simplest form.
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by the HCF.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – percentage to decimal
modelled_examples.question: Convert 37.5% to a decimal.
modelled_examples.explanation: Move the decimal point two places left.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – fraction to percentage
modelled_examples.question: Convert &frac{7}{20} to a percentage.
modelled_examples.explanation: Or multiply top and bottom to get denominator 100.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – decimal to percentage
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.065 to a percentage.
modelled_examples.explanation: Move decimal point two places right.

practice.instruction: Convert to a fraction in simplest form.

practice.instruction: Convert each percentage to a decimal.

043-adding-and-subtracting-decimals.title:
DECIMALS,
(ADDING AND SUBTRACTING DECIMALS)
043-adding-and-subtracting-decimals.objective: LO: I can add and subtract decimals using column methods, lining up the decimal points.

content.text: When adding or subtracting decimals, line up the decimal points so that digits with the same place value are in the same column.
Tip: Use trailing zeros as placeholders so all numbers have the same number of decimal places.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Line up the decimal points. Fill empty places with zeros. Then add or subtract as normal.
key_idea.caption: Pad with zeros to match decimal places

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – adding
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 4.3 + 2.8
modelled_examples.explanation: Carry works exactly the same as with whole numbers.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – different decimal places
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 5.6 + 3.45
modelled_examples.explanation: Pad 5.6 with a zero to make 5.60.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – subtraction
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 8.2 − 3.7
modelled_examples.explanation: Borrow from the next column just like whole numbers.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – from a whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 10 − 3.46
modelled_examples.explanation: Write 10 as 10.00 to subtract easily.

questions.expression: Rope 8 m; cut off 2.35 m. Left?

items.statement: Line up decimal points when adding

044-dividing-decimals.title:
DECIMALS,
(DIVIDING DECIMALS)
044-dividing-decimals.objective: LO: I can divide decimal numbers by whole numbers and by other decimals.

content.text: To divide a decimal by a whole number, use short/long division keeping the decimal point in the same position in the answer.
Dividing by a decimal: Multiply both numbers by 10 (or 100) to make the divisor a whole number, then divide as normal.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: If dividing by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 or 100 to make the divisor a whole number.
key_idea.caption: Make the divisor whole

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – decimal by whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 9.6 ÷ 4
modelled_examples.explanation: The decimal point stays in the same place.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – by a single-digit
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 15.75 ÷ 5
modelled_examples.explanation: Work digit by digit; carry remainders.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – dividing by a decimal
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 4.8 ÷ 0.6
modelled_examples.explanation: Equivalent division: both ×10 doesn't change the answer.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – dividing by 0.2
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 7.5 ÷ 0.25
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply by 100 because the divisor has 2 decimal places.

practice.heading: More decimal ÷ whole number
practice.instruction: Keep the decimal point in line.

items.statement: Multiply both by 10 to remove decimal divisor
When dividing by 0.5, the answer is smaller

A car uses 5.6 litres of fuel per 100 km. How far can it travel on 42 litres? Give your answer to the nearest km.

045-multiplying-decimals.title:
DECIMALS,
(MULTIPLYING DECIMALS)
045-multiplying-decimals.objective: LO: I can multiply decimal numbers using place value and the column method.

content.text: To multiply decimals, ignore the decimal points, multiply as whole numbers, then put the point back using the total number of decimal places.
Rule: Count the total decimal places in the question. The answer has the same total number of decimal places.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply as whole numbers, then place the decimal point so the answer has the correct total number of decimal places.
key_idea.caption: 2 decimal places in total

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – decimal by whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 3.4 × 5
modelled_examples.explanation: One decimal place in the question means one in the answer.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – decimal by decimal
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 0.6 × 0.7
modelled_examples.explanation: Two decimal places total: answer is 0.42 not 4.2.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – with zeros
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 0.05 × 0.4
modelled_examples.explanation: Three decimal places needed; 020 becomes 0.020 = 0.02.

practice.heading: Harder multiplications
practice.instruction: Work as whole numbers first, then place the point.

questions.expression: A tile is 0.3 m × 0.3 m. What is its area?

items.statement: Total d.p. in answer = sum of d.p. in question
Multiplying decimals always gives a bigger number

problems.text: A square has side length 3.5 cm. Find its area. Then find the area of a square with side 0.35 cm. How many times smaller is the second area?
Without a calculator, work out 2.4 × 3.5 and 0.24 × 35. Explain why the answers are the same. What about 24 × 0.35?

046-rounding-decimals-to-decimal-places.title:
DECIMALS,
(ROUNDING DECIMALS TO DECIMAL PLACES)
046-rounding-decimals-to-decimal-places.objective: LO: I can round decimal numbers to a given number of decimal places.

content.text: Rounding to decimal places (d.p.) means shortening a decimal to a given number of digits after the decimal point.
Rule: Look at the NEXT digit. If it is 5 or more, round up. If less than 5, round down (keep the same).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Look at the digit AFTER the one you want. 5 or above: round up. Below 5: round down.
key_idea.equation: 3.147 to 2 d.p. → look at 7 (third d.p.) ≥ 5 → 3.15
key_idea.caption: Critical digit decides

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – rounding to 1 d.p.
modelled_examples.question: Round 4.63 to 1 decimal place.
steps: We want 1 d.p.: keep one digit after the point
modelled_examples.explanation: The digit after is 3 (less than 5), so we keep 4.6.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – rounding to 2 d.p.
modelled_examples.question: Round 7.386 to 2 decimal places.
steps: We want 2 d.p.: keep two digits after the point
modelled_examples.explanation: The 6 forces the previous digit (8) to round up to 9.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – rounding up carries
modelled_examples.question: Round 2.997 to 2 decimal places.
modelled_examples.explanation: Rounding can carry through: 2.99 + 0.01 = 3.00.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – to 3 d.p.
modelled_examples.question: Round 0.12345 to 3 decimal places.
modelled_examples.explanation: The fourth decimal digit (4) is less than 5.

practice.heading: Mixed rounding
practice.instruction: Round to the number of d.p. stated.

items.statement: Look at the digit you want to keep, not the next one

problems.text: A calculator shows 7 ÷ 6 = 1.1666666... Round this to 1, 2, and 3 decimal places. What pattern do you notice?
A measurement is 3.45 cm rounded to 2 d.p. What are the minimum and maximum values the actual measurement could be? (This is the error interval.)

047-bidmas-bodmas.title:
NUMBER OPERATIONS,
(BIDMAS / BODMAS)
047-bidmas-bodmas.objective: LO: I can apply the correct order of operations (BIDMAS) to evaluate expressions.

content.text: BIDMAS tells us the order: Brackets, Indices, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction.
Key point: Division and multiplication are equal priority (left to right). Addition and subtraction are equal priority (left to right).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Always follow BIDMAS: Brackets first, then Indices (powers), then Division/Multiplication (L to R), then Addition/Subtraction (L to R).
key_idea.caption: Brackets, Indices, Divide/Multiply, Add/Subtract

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – multiplication before addition
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 5 + 3 × 4
modelled_examples.explanation: Without brackets, × and ÷ always come before + and −.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – brackets first
modelled_examples.question: Calculate (8 + 2) × 3
modelled_examples.explanation: Brackets override the normal priority.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – indices
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 4 + 3² × 2
modelled_examples.explanation: Indices before multiplication, multiplication before addition.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – complex expression
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)² ÷ 7
modelled_examples.explanation: Work through BIDMAS step by step.

practice.heading: With indices
practice.instruction: Remember: indices come after brackets but before × and ÷.

problems.text: Insert brackets to make each statement true: (i) 3 + 4 × 5 = 35, (ii) 12 ÷ 2 + 4 = 2, (iii) 2 + 3² = 25.
Using the digits 2, 3, 4, 5 (each exactly once) and the operations +, −, ×, ÷, write an expression that equals 1. You may use brackets.

048-checking-answers-using-inverse-opera.title:
NUMBER OPERATIONS,
(CHECKING ANSWERS USING INVERSE OPERATIONS)
048-checking-answers-using-inverse-opera.objective: LO: I can use inverse operations to check calculations and verify my answers.

content.text: Inverse operations are operations that undo each other. Addition undoes subtraction. Multiplication undoes division.
Checking: After solving a calculation, use the inverse to check. If 45 + 32 = 77, then 77 − 32 should = 45.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Use the inverse operation on your answer to get back to the starting number. If you do, your answer is correct.
key_idea.caption: Inverse undoes the operation

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – checking addition
modelled_examples.question: Check: 156 + 89 = 245
modelled_examples.explanation: Subtract one addend from the sum; you should get the other.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – checking multiplication
modelled_examples.question: Check: 23 × 15 = 345
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide the product by one factor; you should get the other.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – finding an error
modelled_examples.question: Check: 64 ÷ 8 = 9
modelled_examples.explanation: The inverse check reveals the error: 64 ÷ 8 = 8.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – checking subtraction
modelled_examples.question: Check: 500 − 237 = 263
modelled_examples.explanation: Add the result to the subtracted number; you should get the original.

practice.heading: Check additions
practice.instruction: Use inverse (subtraction) to check. Write correct or incorrect.

practice.heading: Mixed checking
practice.instruction: Check each calculation using the inverse. State correct or give the right answer.

items.statement: The inverse of addition is subtraction
The inverse of multiplication is addition
The inverse of squaring is dividing by 2

049-multi-step-calculations.title:
NUMBER OPERATIONS,
(MULTI-STEP CALCULATIONS)
049-multi-step-calculations.objective: LO: I can solve problems that require more than one step, choosing the correct operations.

content.text: A multi-step calculation requires you to perform two or more operations in sequence to reach the answer.
Strategy: Read the problem carefully. Identify what you need to find. Break it into smaller steps. Use BIDMAS when needed.

examples.expr: Use BIDMAS for order of operations
Just do operations left to right
Only use one operation per problem

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Break the problem into steps. Solve each step in order. Check your answer makes sense.
key_idea.caption: One step at a time

modelled_examples.question: You pay for a £7.80 item with a £20 note. How many 50p coins in your change?
modelled_examples.explanation: Find the change first, then divide by the coin value.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – distance/speed
modelled_examples.question: A car travels at 60 mph for 2.5 hours then 40 mph for 1.5 hours. Total distance?
modelled_examples.explanation: Distance = speed × time for each section, then add.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – profit calculation
modelled_examples.question: Buy 50 items at £3 each. Sell 40 at £5 and 10 at £2. Total profit?
modelled_examples.explanation: Profit = revenue − cost.

050-adding-and-subtracting-fractions.title:
FRACTIONS (SECONDARY),
(ADDING AND SUBTRACTING FRACTIONS)
050-adding-and-subtracting-fractions.objective: LO: I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators by finding a common denominator.

content.text: To add or subtract fractions with different denominators, first find a common denominator (usually the LCM), then add/subtract the numerators.
Steps: 1) Find the LCM of denominators. 2) Convert both fractions. 3) Add/subtract numerators. 4) Simplify.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Same denominator: just add/subtract numerators. Different: find the LCM first.
key_idea.caption: Cross-multiply method (or use LCM)

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – same denominator
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{8} + &frac{2}{8}
modelled_examples.explanation: When denominators match, just add the tops.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – different denominators
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{2}{3} + &frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert both to twelfths, then add.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – subtraction
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{5}{6} − &frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Same method: common denominator, then subtract numerators.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed numbers
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 1&frac{1}{2} + 2&frac{2}{3}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert to improper fractions, find common denominator, then convert back.

practice.instruction: Add or subtract. Simplify if possible.

practice.heading: Subtraction with different denominators
practice.instruction: Find a common denominator, then subtract.

practice.instruction: Calculate. Give answers in simplest form.

items.statement: You need a common denominator to add fractions

051-algebraic-fractions.title:
FRACTIONS (SECONDARY),
(ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS)
051-algebraic-fractions.objective: LO: I can simplify, add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic fractions.

content.text: An algebraic fraction has expressions with letters in the numerator, denominator, or both (e.g. &frac{x+2}{3} or &frac{2x}{x−1}).
Same rules: All fraction rules still apply. To add/subtract, find common denominator. To simplify, cancel common factors.

examples.desc: cannot cancel part of a sum

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Treat algebraic fractions like number fractions. Factorise first, then cancel common factors.
key_idea.caption: Factorise numerator, then cancel

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simplifying
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{8x}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Cancel the common factor of 4.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – adding
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x}{3} + &frac{x}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply each fraction to get denominator 12.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – subtracting
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{2x}{5} − &frac{x}{3}
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply tops and bottoms to get a common denominator.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – factorising to simplify
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x² + 3x}{x}
modelled_examples.explanation: Factorise first, then cancel the common factor.

practice.instruction: Find a common denominator and add.

practice.heading: Subtracting algebraic fractions
practice.instruction: Find a common denominator and subtract.

practice.instruction: Factorise the numerator or denominator, then cancel.

052-dividing-fractions.title:
FRACTIONS (SECONDARY),
(DIVIDING FRACTIONS)
052-dividing-fractions.objective: LO: I can divide fractions by flipping the second fraction and multiplying (KFC method).

content.text: To divide by a fraction, Keep the first fraction, Flip the second (reciprocal), then Change to multiplication (KFC).
Reciprocal: The reciprocal of &frac{a}{b} is &frac{b}{a}. Flip the fraction upside down.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Keep the first fraction. Flip the second. Change ÷ to ×.
key_idea.caption: KFC: Keep, Flip, Change

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – basic division
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{4} ÷ &frac{1}{2}
modelled_examples.explanation: Flip the second fraction then multiply across.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – dividing by a whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{2}{5} ÷ 3
modelled_examples.explanation: A whole number n = &frac{n}{1}. Its reciprocal is &frac{1}{n}.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – both improper
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{5}{6} ÷ &frac{5}{3}
modelled_examples.explanation: Cancel before multiplying if possible: &frac{5}{6} × &frac{3}{5} = &frac{1}{2}.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed numbers
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 2&frac{1}{2} ÷ 1&frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

practice.instruction: Write the whole number as a fraction first.

practice.heading: Both proper fractions
practice.instruction: Keep, Flip, Change. Simplify your answer.

053-multiplying-fractions.title:
FRACTIONS (SECONDARY),
(MULTIPLYING FRACTIONS)
053-multiplying-fractions.objective: LO: I can multiply fractions and mixed numbers, simplifying my answers.

content.text: To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Simplify at the end (or cancel first).
Tip: Cross-cancel before multiplying to keep numbers small. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply tops together, multiply bottoms together. Cancel common factors for simpler working.
key_idea.caption: Straight across: top × top, bottom × bottom

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simple multiplication
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{2}{5} × &frac{3}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 2.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – cancelling first
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{8} × &frac{4}{9}
steps: Cancel: 3 and 9 share factor 3; 4 and 8 share factor 4
modelled_examples.explanation: Cross-cancel before multiplying keeps numbers small.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – fraction of a whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{4} × 20
modelled_examples.explanation: 3/4 of 20: divide by 4 (=5), multiply by 3 (=15).

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed numbers
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 1&frac{2}{3} × 2&frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Always convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying.

practice.heading: Fraction of a whole number
practice.instruction: Find each fraction of the number.

practice.heading: Mixed multiplication
practice.instruction: Calculate. Give answers in simplest form.

items.statement: You need a common denominator to multiply

problems.text: A rectangle has width &frac{3}{4} m and length 1&frac{2}{3} m. Find its area. Then find the area of a square with side &frac{5}{6} m.

Show that &frac{a}{b} × &frac{b}{a} = 1 for any non-zero a and b. What is the name for &frac{b}{a} in relation to &frac{a}{b}? Use this to explain why dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

066-adding-and-subtracting-fractions-dif.title:
FRACTIONS ALL OPERATIONS,
(ADDING AND SUBTRACTING FRACTIONS - DIFFERENT DENOMINATORS)
066-adding-and-subtracting-fractions-dif.objective: LO: I can add and subtract fractions with different denominators by finding a common denominator.

content.text: To add or subtract fractions with different denominators, we must first find a common denominator so that both fractions have the same-sized parts.
Remember: Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of the denominators, convert both fractions, then add or subtract the numerators.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Find the LCM of the denominators, convert each fraction to equivalent fractions, then add or subtract numerators.
key_idea.caption: Cross-multiply to find equivalent numerators

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – adding unit fractions
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{1}{3} + &frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert both fractions to twelfths, then add numerators.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – subtracting fractions
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{4} - &frac{2}{5}
modelled_examples.explanation: Same process: find common denominator, then subtract.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – adding with simplifying
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{2}{3} + &frac{1}{6}
modelled_examples.explanation: When one denominator is a factor of the other, only convert one fraction.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed numbers
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 1&frac{1}{3} + 2&frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

practice.heading: Adding fractions (unit)
practice.instruction: Find a common denominator and add.

practice.heading: Mixed numbers
practice.instruction: Add or subtract the mixed numbers.

practice.heading: Mixed practice
practice.instruction: Add or subtract. Simplify your answer.

items.statement: To add fractions we need a common denominator

problems.text: A recipe needs &frac{2}{3} cup of flour and &frac{3}{4} cup of sugar. How much more sugar than flour is needed? What is the total amount of flour and sugar combined?
Aisha walks 1&frac{1}{4} km to school and 1&frac{2}{3} km to her friend's house. How far does she walk in total? How much further is it to her friend's house than to school?

067-dividing-fractions.title:
FRACTIONS ALL OPERATIONS,
(DIVIDING FRACTIONS)
067-dividing-fractions.objective: LO: I can divide fractions by flipping the second fraction and multiplying.

content.text: To divide by a fraction, we keep, change, flip: keep the first fraction, change division to multiplication, and flip (find the reciprocal of) the second fraction.
Remember: The reciprocal of &frac{a}{b} is &frac{b}{a}. Dividing by a fraction makes the answer bigger.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Keep the first fraction, change the operation to multiplication, flip the second fraction.
key_idea.caption: Keep, Change, Flip

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simple division
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{2}{3} ÷ &frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Flip the second fraction then multiply across.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – both non-unit
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{5} ÷ &frac{2}{7}
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply numerators and denominators separately.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – dividing by a whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{4}{5} ÷ 2
modelled_examples.explanation: A whole number is just a fraction with denominator 1.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed numbers
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 1&frac{1}{2} ÷ &frac{3}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

practice.heading: Dividing by whole numbers
practice.instruction: Divide each fraction by the whole number.

items.statement: To divide by a fraction, flip the second fraction and multiply
Dividing by a fraction always gives a smaller answer

problems.text: A ribbon is &frac{3}{4} m long. It is cut into pieces that are each &frac{1}{8} m long. How many pieces can be cut? If each piece costs 25p, what is the total cost?
A jug holds 2&frac{1}{2} litres of juice. Each glass holds &frac{1}{3} litre. How many full glasses can be poured? How much juice is left over?

068-fractions-of-amounts.title:
FRACTIONS ALL OPERATIONS,
(FRACTIONS OF AMOUNTS)
068-fractions-of-amounts.objective: LO: I can find a fraction of a given amount by dividing and multiplying.

key_terms.title: Finding a fraction of an amount

content.text: To find a fraction of an amount, divide the amount by the denominator then multiply by the numerator.
Method: &frac{a}{b} of n = n ÷ b × a. Always divide first to keep numbers small.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Divide by the denominator first to find one part, then multiply by the numerator to find the required number of parts.
key_idea.equation: &frac{a}{b} of n = n ÷ b × a
key_idea.caption: Divide by bottom, multiply by top

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – unit fraction
modelled_examples.question: Find &frac{1}{5} of 45
modelled_examples.explanation: For unit fractions, just divide by the denominator.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – non-unit fraction
modelled_examples.question: Find &frac{3}{4} of 60
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top number.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – fraction of money
modelled_examples.question: Find &frac{2}{3} of £18
modelled_examples.explanation: Same method works for money and measurements.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – finding the whole
modelled_examples.question: &frac{3}{5} of a number is 24. Find the number.
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide by the numerator to find one part, then multiply by the denominator.

practice.heading: Unit fractions of amounts
practice.instruction: Find each fraction of the amount.

practice.heading: Non-unit fractions
practice.instruction: Find the fraction of each amount.

practice.instruction: Find the fraction of each amount.

practice.instruction: Work backwards to find the original amount.

To find the whole, divide by numerator then multiply by denominator

069-multiplying-fractions.title:
FRACTIONS ALL OPERATIONS,
(MULTIPLYING FRACTIONS)
069-multiplying-fractions.objective: LO: I can multiply fractions and mixed numbers by multiplying numerators and denominators.

content.text: To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together. Simplify if possible.
Tip: You can cross-cancel before multiplying to keep numbers small.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Simplify the result.
key_idea.caption: Top times top, bottom times bottom

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simple multiplication
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{2}{5} × &frac{3}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Always simplify your final answer.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – cross-cancelling
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{8} × &frac{4}{9}
modelled_examples.explanation: Cross-cancelling makes the multiplication simpler.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – multiplying by a whole number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate &frac{3}{7} × 5
modelled_examples.explanation: Write whole numbers as fractions with denominator 1.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed numbers
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 1&frac{1}{3} × 2&frac{1}{4}
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert to improper fractions, then cross-cancel.

items.statement: Multiplying fractions always gives a bigger number

problems.text: A rectangular garden is 4&frac{1}{2} m long and 2&frac{2}{3} m wide. Find the area. If fencing costs £8 per metre, how much does it cost to fence the perimeter?
In a class of 30 pupils, &frac{2}{5} are boys. Of the boys, &frac{3}{4} play football. What fraction of the whole class are boys who play football? How many pupils is this?

070-adding-and-subtracting-algebraic-fra.title:
ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS,
(ADDING AND SUBTRACTING ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS)
070-adding-and-subtracting-algebraic-fra.objective: LO: I can add and subtract algebraic fractions by finding a common denominator.

content.text: An algebraic fraction has a variable (letter) in the numerator, denominator, or both. To add or subtract them, we need a common denominator, just like with number fractions.
Strategy: Find the LCM of the denominators, convert each fraction, then add or subtract the numerators.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Find the lowest common denominator (LCD), rewrite each fraction over the LCD, then combine the numerators.
key_idea.caption: Cross-multiply to find common denominator xy

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – same denominator
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{3}{x} + &frac{5}{x}
modelled_examples.explanation: When denominators match, simply add the numerators.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – different single-term denominators
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{2}{x} + &frac{3}{y}
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply each fraction by the other denominator over itself.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – linear denominators
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{1}{x + 1} + &frac{2}{x + 3}
modelled_examples.explanation: Expand the numerators carefully, then collect like terms.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – subtraction
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{5}{x+2} − &frac{3}{x+1}
modelled_examples.explanation: With subtraction, distribute the minus sign carefully.

practice.heading: Different single-term denominators
practice.instruction: Find a common denominator and simplify.

practice.heading: Linear expression denominators
practice.instruction: Simplify. Write as a single fraction.

practice.heading: Mixed algebraic fractions
practice.instruction: Write as a single fraction in simplest form.

items.statement: To add fractions with different denominators, find the LCM first

problems.text: Show that &frac{1}{x−1} − &frac{1}{x+1} simplifies to &frac{2}{x²−1}. Hence find the value when x = 5.
Simplify &frac{x+1}{x+2} + &frac{x+3}{x+4} and write your answer as a single fraction. What value(s) of x would make this expression undefined?

071-equations-involving-fractions.title:
ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS,
(EQUATIONS INVOLVING FRACTIONS)
071-equations-involving-fractions.objective: LO: I can solve equations that contain algebraic fractions.

content.text: An equation involving fractions has the unknown in a fraction. The key strategy is to multiply through by the LCD to eliminate denominators.
Strategy: Find the LCD of all fractions, multiply every term by it, then solve the resulting equation.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply every term by the LCD to clear fractions, then solve the equation as normal.
key_idea.caption: Multiply all terms by LCD = 6

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – single fraction
modelled_examples.question: Solve &frac{x}{4} = 7
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply by the denominator to isolate x.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – two fractions
modelled_examples.question: Solve &frac{x}{2} + &frac{x}{5} = 7
modelled_examples.explanation: After clearing fractions, collect terms and solve.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – x in denominator
modelled_examples.question: Solve &frac{6}{x} = 3
modelled_examples.explanation: When x is in the denominator, multiply both sides by x.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – cross-multiplication
modelled_examples.question: Solve &frac{x+1}{3} = &frac{x−2}{2}
modelled_examples.explanation: Cross-multiply when you have a fraction equal to a fraction.

items.statement: To clear fractions, multiply every term by the LCD
Cross-multiply means a/b = c/d gives ad = bc

problems.text: Solve &frac{2}{x+1} + &frac{3}{x+2} = 1. Show all your working and check your answer by substitution.
The sum of a number and its reciprocal is &frac{5}{2}. Write this as an equation and solve it to find the two possible values of the number.

072-multiplying-and-dividing-algebraic-f.title:
ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS,
(MULTIPLYING AND DIVIDING ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS)
072-multiplying-and-dividing-algebraic-f.objective: LO: I can multiply and divide algebraic fractions and simplify the result.

content.text: To multiply algebraic fractions, multiply numerators together and denominators together. To divide, flip the second fraction and multiply.
Strategy: Factorise first where possible, cancel common factors, then multiply what remains.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom. Divide: flip the second fraction then multiply. Always cancel common factors.
key_idea.caption: KFC: Keep, Flip, Change

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simple multiplication
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{3}{x} × &frac{x}{5}
modelled_examples.explanation: Cancel any common factors between numerator and denominator.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – division
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{4}{x} ÷ &frac{2}{x}
modelled_examples.explanation: Keep the first, flip the second, then multiply.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – factorising first
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x²+x}{x+1} × &frac{2}{x}
modelled_examples.explanation: Always factorise before cancelling to spot common factors.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – harder division
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x+3}{x−1} ÷ &frac{x+3}{x+2}
modelled_examples.explanation: After flipping, cancel the common factor (x+3).

items.statement: To divide fractions, flip the second and multiply

problems.text: Simplify &frac{x² − 4}{x² + 5x + 6} × &frac{x + 3}{x − 2}. Factorise all quadratics fully before cancelling.
Show that &frac{x² − 9}{x + 1} ÷ &frac{x² − 6x + 9}{x² + x} simplifies to &frac{x(x + 3)}{x − 3}.

073-simplifying-algebraic-fractions.title:
ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS,
(SIMPLIFYING ALGEBRAIC FRACTIONS)
073-simplifying-algebraic-fractions.objective: LO: I can simplify algebraic fractions by factorising and cancelling common factors.

content.text: To simplify an algebraic fraction, factorise the numerator and denominator, then cancel common factors.
Strategy: Look for common numerical factors first, then factorise any quadratic or linear expressions.

examples.desc: cannot cancel x from a sum
x²+1 does not factorise over x

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Factorise numerator and denominator completely, then cancel any factors that appear in both.
key_idea.caption: Cancel the common factor (x + 2)

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – common numerical factor
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{6x}{9}
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by their HCF.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – common variable factor
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x² + 3x}{x}
modelled_examples.explanation: Factorise the numerator to reveal the common factor.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – difference of two squares
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x² − 9}{x + 3}
modelled_examples.explanation: Recognise the difference of two squares pattern: a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b).

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – quadratic numerator
modelled_examples.question: Simplify &frac{x² + 5x + 6}{x + 2}
modelled_examples.explanation: Factorise the quadratic to find the common factor with the denominator.

problems.text: Simplify &frac{x² + 2x − 15}{x² − 9} fully. State any values of x for which the fraction is undefined.
Show that &frac{2x² + 7x + 3}{2x² + 5x + 2} simplifies to &frac{x + 3}{x + 2}. Explain each factorisation step.

078-converting-between-fdp.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES
(CONVERTING BETWEEN FDP)
078-converting-between-fdp.objective: LO: I can convert fluently between fractions, decimals and percentages.

content.text: Converting means writing a number in a DIFFERENT form without changing its value. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways to write the same amount.
Key fact: To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Fraction → Decimal: divide top by bottom. Decimal → Percentage: × 100. Percentage → Fraction: write over 100 and simplify.
key_idea.caption: Divide, then multiply by 100

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – fraction to decimal
modelled_examples.question: Convert ¾ to a decimal
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide numerator by denominator: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – decimal to percentage
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.35 to a percentage
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply the decimal by 100 and add the % symbol.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – percentage to fraction
modelled_examples.question: Convert 45% to a fraction in simplest form
modelled_examples.explanation: Write over 100, then simplify by dividing both by the HCF (5).

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – fraction to percentage
modelled_examples.question: Convert &frac{7}{20} to a percentage
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert to decimal first (divide), then multiply by 100.

practice.heading: Fraction to decimal
practice.instruction: Convert each fraction to a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator.

practice.heading: Decimal to percentage
practice.instruction: Convert each decimal to a percentage by multiplying by 100.

practice.heading: Percentage to fraction
practice.instruction: Convert each percentage to a fraction in its simplest form. Write over 100 then simplify.

practice.heading: Fraction to percentage
practice.instruction: Convert each fraction to a percentage. Divide first, then multiply by 100.

practice.heading: Mixed conversions
practice.instruction: Convert each value to the other two forms (fraction, decimal, percentage).

079-ordering-fdp.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES
(ORDERING FDP)
079-ordering-fdp.objective: LO: I can order fractions, decimals and percentages by converting to a common form.

content.text: Ordering FDP means arranging fractions, decimals and percentages from SMALLEST to largest (ascending) or largest to smallest (descending).
Strategy: Convert ALL values to the SAME form (usually decimals) before comparing. Then rewrite in original form for your final answer.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Convert everything to decimals. Compare digit by digit from left to right. Write your final answer in the ORIGINAL forms given in the question.
key_idea.caption: Ascending: 30%, 0.34, ⅜

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – two values
modelled_examples.question: Which is larger: ⅗ or 55%?
modelled_examples.explanation: Convert both to decimals: 0.6 > 0.55, so ⅗ is larger.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – three values ascending
modelled_examples.question: Order: 0.7, ¾, 72%
modelled_examples.explanation: All as decimals: 0.7, 0.75, 0.72. Ascending: 0.7, 0.72, 0.75.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – tricky decimals
modelled_examples.question: Order: 0.3, ⅓, 30%
modelled_examples.explanation: ⅓ = 0.333... which is greater than 0.3. Note: 0.3 and 30% are equal.

practice.heading: Convert to decimals
practice.instruction: Convert each value to a decimal so you can compare them.

practice.heading: Compare two values
practice.instruction: Write < or > between each pair. Convert to decimals first.

practice.instruction: Write these in ascending order. Show your decimal conversions.

practice.heading: Order descending (largest first)
practice.instruction: Write these in descending order. Show your decimal conversions.

practice.instruction: Order these sets. State whether ascending or descending as indicated.

Small: ⅗ full for 80p   Medium: 58% full for 75p   Large: 0.55 full for 70p

080-percentage-change.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES,
(PERCENTAGE CHANGE)
080-percentage-change.objective: LO: I can calculate percentage increase, decrease and percentage change.

content.text: Percentage change measures how much a value has increased or decreased as a percentage of the original.
Formula: % change = (change ÷ original) × 100. Always divide by the ORIGINAL amount, not the new amount.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: % change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Positive = increase, negative = decrease.
key_idea.caption: Always divide by ORIGINAL

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – increase
modelled_examples.question: Price rises from £40 to £50. Find the % increase.
modelled_examples.explanation: Always divide the change by the ORIGINAL price (£40).

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – decrease
modelled_examples.question: Population drops from 800 to 600. Find the % decrease.
modelled_examples.explanation: The change is always positive; the ‘decrease’ describes the direction.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – from amounts
modelled_examples.question: A coat costs £80 in a sale. The original price was £100. % change?
modelled_examples.explanation: Negative answer means a decrease.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – growth
modelled_examples.question: Plant grows from 12 cm to 18 cm. % growth?
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide the increase by the original (12 cm).

practice.heading: % increase
practice.instruction: Calculate the percentage increase. Use (change ÷ old) × 100.

practice.heading: Word problems
practice.instruction: State whether each is an increase or decrease, and find the %.

practice.heading: Mixed % change
practice.instruction: Find the percentage change. State increase or decrease.

items.statement: Divide by the new value, not the old
% change can be negative for a decrease

081-recurring-decimals.title:
FRACTIONS, DECIMALS AND PERCENTAGES
(RECURRING DECIMALS)
081-recurring-decimals.objective: LO: I can convert recurring decimals to fractions using algebraic methods.

content.text: Recurring decimals have one or more digits that REPEAT forever. We write a dot above the repeating digit(s): 0.3̇ means 0.333... and 0.1̇2̇ means 0.121212...
Key fact: Every recurring decimal can be written as an exact fraction. Terminating decimals have denominators whose only prime factors are 2 and 5.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Let x = the recurring decimal. Multiply by 10 (or 100, 1000...) to shift the repeating block. Subtract to eliminate the recurring part. Solve for x.
key_idea.caption: Multiply, subtract, simplify

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – one repeating digit
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.4̇ to a fraction
modelled_examples.explanation: One repeating digit: multiply by 10. Subtract x from 10x to get 9x = 4.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – two repeating digits
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.6̇3̇ to a fraction
modelled_examples.explanation: Two repeating digits: multiply by 100. Subtract: 99x = 63. Simplify: 63/99 = 7/11.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – non-repeating start
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.16̇ to a fraction
modelled_examples.explanation: The 1 doesn’t repeat, but the 6 does. Use 100x − 10x = 90x to eliminate the recurring part.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – three repeating digits
modelled_examples.question: Convert 0.1̇23̇ to a fraction
modelled_examples.explanation: Three repeating digits: multiply by 1000. Subtract: 999x = 123. Simplify: 123/999 = 41/333.

practice.heading: Identify the recurring part
practice.instruction: Write the first 6 decimal places and underline the repeating block.

practice.heading: One repeating digit → fraction
practice.instruction: Convert each recurring decimal to a fraction. Simplify where possible.

practice.heading: Two repeating digits → fraction
practice.instruction: Convert each recurring decimal to a fraction. Use ×100 and subtract.

practice.heading: Non-repeating start → fraction
practice.instruction: Convert each recurring decimal to a fraction. Careful: part of the decimal doesn’t repeat.

items.statement: 0.1̇2̇ means multiply by 100 to shift the block
0.16̇ needs 100x − 10x to eliminate the recurring part

problems.text:

A student says “&frac17; = 0.142857̇” (with a dot only over the 7).
Explain why this is wrong. What is the correct dot notation for &frac17;? How many digits repeat?

082-sketching-quadratic-cubic-and-recipr.title:
FUNCTIONS AND GRAPHS,
(SKETCHING QUADRATIC, CUBIC AND RECIPROCAL GRAPHS)
082-sketching-quadratic-cubic-and-recipr.objective: LO: I can recognise and sketch quadratic, cubic and reciprocal graphs from their equations.

content.text: A quadratic graph (y = ax² + bx + c) forms a U-shape (parabola). A cubic graph (y = ax³) has an S-shape. A reciprocal graph (y = &frac{a}{x}) has two separate curves.
Key features: Look for the y-intercept, turning points, and asymptotes to sketch each graph accurately.

examples.expr: y = x² is a U-shaped parabola
y = x³ passes through the origin with S-shape
y = &frac{1}{x} has two branches in Q1 and Q3
y = x² is a straight line

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: The highest power of x tells you the shape: x² = parabola, x³ = cubic curve, &frac{1}{x} = reciprocal (hyperbola).
key_idea.caption: a determines direction, c is the y-intercept

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – quadratic graph
modelled_examples.question: Sketch y = x² - 4
steps: x-intercepts: x² = 4, so x = 2 and x = -2
modelled_examples.answer: U-shape crossing x-axis at (-2, 0) and (2, 0), vertex at (0, -4)
modelled_examples.explanation: The -4 shifts the parabola down by 4 units.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – negative quadratic
modelled_examples.question: Sketch y = -x² + 9
modelled_examples.answer: Inverted U with maximum at (0, 9), crossing at (-3, 0) and (3, 0)
modelled_examples.explanation: Negative coefficient of x² flips the parabola.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – cubic graph
modelled_examples.question: Sketch y = x³ - x
steps: Shape: S-curve (positive x³) through these three roots
modelled_examples.explanation: Factorising helps find where the cubic crosses the x-axis.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – reciprocal graph
modelled_examples.question: Sketch y = &frac{3}{x}
steps: When x = 1, y = 3; when x = 3, y = 1
When x = -1, y = -3; curves in Q1 and Q3
modelled_examples.answer: Two branches: one in Q1, one in Q3, never touching the axes
modelled_examples.explanation: The graph gets closer to the axes but never reaches them.

083-transformations-of-graphs.title:
FUNCTIONS AND GRAPHS,
(TRANSFORMATIONS OF GRAPHS)
083-transformations-of-graphs.objective: LO: I can describe and apply translations, reflections and stretches to graphs of functions.

content.text: A transformation changes the position or shape of a graph. Key types: translations (shifts), reflections (flips), and stretches (scaling).
Notation: f(x) + a shifts up, f(x + a) shifts left, -f(x) reflects in x-axis, f(-x) reflects in y-axis.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Changes inside the bracket affect x (horizontal, opposite direction). Changes outside affect y (vertical, same direction).
key_idea.caption: a = vertical stretch, b = horizontal shift (opposite), c = vertical shift

modelled_examples.explanation: Inside the bracket, the shift is in the opposite direction.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – reflection in x-axis
modelled_examples.question: Describe the transformation from y = x³ to y = -x³
steps: The negative is outside: reflects in x-axis
modelled_examples.explanation: All positive y-values become negative and vice versa.

modelled_examples.question: Describe the transformation from y = sin x to y = 3 sin x
modelled_examples.explanation: Every y-coordinate is multiplied by 3.

085-double-inequalities.title:
INEQUALITIES,
(DOUBLE INEQUALITIES)
085-double-inequalities.objective: LO: I can solve and represent double (compound) inequalities.

content.text: A double inequality has the variable between two bounds, e.g. 3 < x ≤ 7. It means x is greater than 3 AND less than or equal to 7 simultaneously.
Strategy: Solve by performing the same operation to all three parts of the inequality.

examples.expr: 2 < x ≤ 5 means x can be 3, 4, or 5 (integers)
To solve, only work on the middle part
examples.desc: must do same to all three parts

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Whatever you do to the middle, do the same to the left and right. If you multiply/divide by a negative, reverse both inequality signs.
key_idea.equation: a < bx + c ≤ d ⇒ &frac{a − c}{b} < x ≤ &frac{d − c}{b}
key_idea.caption: Subtract c, then divide by b (all three parts)

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – listing integers
modelled_examples.question: List the integers satisfying −2 < x ≤ 3
steps: x must be greater than −2 (not including −2)
x must be less than or equal to 3
modelled_examples.explanation: Open circle at −2 (not included), closed at 3 (included).

modelled_examples.explanation: Perform identical operations on all three parts.

modelled_examples.explanation: Dividing by a negative reverses the inequality signs.

086-inequalities-in-two-variables.title:
INEQUALITIES,
(INEQUALITIES IN TWO VARIABLES)
086-inequalities-in-two-variables.objective: LO: I can represent and identify regions defined by linear inequalities in two variables.

content.text: An inequality in two variables such as y < 2x + 1 defines a region on a coordinate grid, not just a line.
Strategy: Draw the boundary line (dashed for < or >, solid for ≤ or ≥), then shade the correct region by testing a point.

y ≥ 2x − 1: region above and including the line
x + y ≤ 5: test (0,0) gives 0 ≤ 5, true, so shade that side
y < x + 3 uses a solid boundary line
The line y = x is always the boundary for y > x

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Draw the boundary line, choose dashed or solid, then test a point to determine which side to shade.

087-representing-inequalities-on-a-numbe.objective: LO: I can represent linear inequalities on a number line using open and closed circles.

content.text: On a number line, an open circle (○) means the value is NOT included (< or >). A closed circle (●) means the value IS included (≤ or ≥).
Strategy: Solve the inequality first, then draw the number line with the correct circle and arrow/line.

examples.expr: x > 3: open circle at 3, arrow right
x ≤ 5: closed circle at 5, arrow left
2 < x ≤ 6: open at 2, closed at 6, line between

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Open circle = not included (strict). Closed circle = included (or equal to). Arrow shows the direction of valid values.
key_idea.caption: Open = excluded, Closed = included

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – less than or equal

modelled_examples.explanation: No arrows needed for a compound inequality, just the connecting line.

093-4-times-table.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(FOUR TIMES TABLE)
093-4-times-table.objective: LO: I can recall and use the 4 times table to multiply and divide.

content.text: The 4 times table is a list of multiples of 4: numbers we get when we count in 4s. Multiples of 4 are always even, and you can find them by doubling the 2 times table.
Strategy: Skip-count in 4s on your fingers, or use a number line. Each jump adds 4.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiplication is repeated addition. 4 × 4 means ‘4 groups of 4’. You can also think of it as ‘4 groups of 4’ — the answer is the same.
key_idea.caption: Four groups of 4

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – missing factor

modelled_examples.explanation: Divide: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – division by sharing
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 32 ÷ 4
steps: How many groups of 4 fit in 32?
modelled_examples.explanation: Division is the inverse of multiplication.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – word problem

modelled_examples.explanation: Always show your working clearly.

094-8-times-table.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(EIGHT TIMES TABLE)
094-8-times-table.objective: LO: I can recall and use the 8 times table to multiply and divide.

content.text: The 8 times table is a list of multiples of 8: numbers we get when we count in 8s. Multiples of 8 are always even, and you can find them by doubling the 4 times table.
Strategy: Skip-count in 8s on your fingers, or use a number line. Each jump adds 8.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiplication is repeated addition. 8 × 4 means ‘4 groups of 8’. You can also think of it as ‘8 groups of 4’ — the answer is the same.
key_idea.caption: Four groups of 8

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – single multiplication
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 4 × 8
modelled_examples.explanation: Skip-count in 8s 4 times to reach 32.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – missing factor
modelled_examples.question: Solve: ___ × 8 = 48
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide: 48 ÷ 8 = 6.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – division by sharing
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 56 ÷ 8

modelled_examples.explanation: Division is the inverse of multiplication.

095-mixed-times-table-practice.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(MIXED TIMES TABLE PRACTICE)
095-mixed-times-table-practice.objective: LO: I can fluently recall and use multiplication and division facts up to 12 × 12.

content.text: Fluency means recalling a multiplication fact in under 2 seconds, without counting on fingers.
Tip: Each multiplication gives you two division facts. e.g. 6×7=42, so 42÷6=7 and 42÷7=6.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiplication is commutative: a × b = b × a. So you only need to learn HALF the table.
key_idea.caption: Same answer either way

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – fact recall
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 7 × 8
modelled_examples.explanation: If you know 7×7=49, just add one more 7.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – missing factor
modelled_examples.question: Solve: 6 × ___ = 54
modelled_examples.explanation: 9 sixes make 54.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – division
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 72 ÷ 9
modelled_examples.explanation: Use multiplication to check: 9 × 8 = 72 ✓

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – two-step
modelled_examples.question: Calculate (4 × 6) + (3 × 7)
modelled_examples.explanation: Do each multiplication first, then add.

practice.heading: Quick recall
practice.instruction: Answer as quickly as you can.
