A school has 11 classes with 12 children in each. On Sports Day, the children form teams of 8. How many full teams can be made? Are any children left over?

096-dividing-by-10-100-and-1000.title:
DIVISION,
(BY 10, 100 AND 1000)
096-dividing-by-10-100-and-1000.objective: LO: I can divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 by shifting place value.

content.text: Dividing by 10 shifts every digit one column RIGHT. The digits stay the same; their place value gets smaller.
Common error: ‘just remove a zero.’ Doesn't work for decimals or numbers without trailing zeros (e.g. 47 ÷ 10 ≠ 47, it's 4.7).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Dividing by 10 = shift digits 1 right. By 100 = shift 2 right. By 1000 = shift 3 right. The decimal point appears to move LEFT.
key_idea.caption: Decimal point moves 2 places left

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – whole ÷ 10
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 80 ÷ 10
modelled_examples.explanation: The 8 moves from tens to ones; the 0 falls off.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – whole ÷ 100
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 4500 ÷ 100
modelled_examples.explanation: Two zeros become placeholders that drop off.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – needs decimal
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 23 ÷ 10
modelled_examples.explanation: We can't just ‘remove a zero’ here — there isn't one.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – decimal ÷ 1000
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 47 ÷ 1000
modelled_examples.explanation: Add zeros as placeholders before the digits.

practice.heading: Two-step
practice.instruction: Apply the rule twice or combine with multiplication.

problems.text: A factory produces 4500 toys a week. They are packed in boxes of 100 toys. How many boxes are made? Use ÷100 to find out.
3.4 km is how many metres? Then divide that answer by 1000 to convert back to km. Show that you get the original number.

097-long-division.title:
DIVISION,
(LONG DIVISION)
097-long-division.objective: LO: I can divide larger numbers using the long division algorithm (bus stop method).

content.text: Long division is a written method for dividing by 2-digit or larger numbers. We work digit-by-digit from left to right.
Bus stop: the divisor sits outside, the dividend underneath, and the answer appears on top. Subtract, bring down, repeat.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Repeat the cycle: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Stop when no more digits to bring down.
key_idea.caption: Repeat until done

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – no remainder
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 672 ÷ 12
modelled_examples.explanation: Answer: 56 (no remainder). Check: 56×12 = 672 ✓

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – with remainder
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 415 ÷ 13
modelled_examples.explanation: 31 remainder 12. Check: 31×13 + 12 = 403+12 = 415 ✓

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – 3-digit divisor
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 4500 ÷ 25
modelled_examples.explanation: Check: 180×25 = 4500 ✓

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – decimal answer
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 35 ÷ 4
steps: Add a decimal point and zero: 30
modelled_examples.explanation: Keep going past decimal point until remainder is 0 or you have enough d.p.

practice.heading: With remainder
practice.instruction: Write the answer as ‘quotient r remainder’.

practice.heading: Decimal answers
practice.instruction: Continue past the decimal point until exact.

items.statement: DMSB stands for Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down
If divisor doesn't fit, skip the digit
Remainder must be smaller than divisor

problems.text: A factory has 2160 chocolates to pack into boxes of 24. How many full boxes? Are any chocolates left over? Show your full long division.
Mr Khan drives 462 miles using 14 gallons of fuel. Find his miles-per-gallon (mpg). Now do 637 miles ÷ 13 gallons. Which trip was more efficient?

098-long-multiplication.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(LONG MULTIPLICATION)
098-long-multiplication.objective: LO: I can multiply 2- and 3-digit numbers using the long multiplication (column) method.

content.text: Long multiplication is the column method for multi-digit × multi-digit. We multiply by each digit separately, then add.
Place-value rule: when multiplying by tens, put a 0 in the units column first. By hundreds, put 00.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply by each digit of the bottom number separately. Each new row shifts left by one column (place value).
key_idea.caption: Two rows, then add

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – 2 by 2 digit
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 23 × 45
modelled_examples.explanation: Always add a placeholder 0 when multiplying by the tens digit.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – with carrying
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 47 × 36
modelled_examples.explanation: Show carries clearly above each column.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – 3 by 2 digit
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 146 × 27
modelled_examples.explanation: 3-digit numbers follow the same rules; just more digits.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – with zeros
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 304 × 25
modelled_examples.explanation: The zero in 304 means ×0 gives 0 in that column.

practice.heading: 2 by 2 digit
practice.instruction: Two rows, then add. Don't forget the placeholder 0.

items.statement: Add a placeholder 0 when multiplying by tens

problems.text: A theatre has 27 rows with 48 seats per row. How many seats in total? If £12.50 per ticket, what's the maximum revenue per show?
A factory packs 148 chocolates per box, 36 boxes per crate, and ships 12 crates a day. How many chocolates ship per day? Show your working clearly.

099-multiplying-by-10-100-and-1000.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(BY 10, 100 AND 1000)
099-multiplying-by-10-100-and-1000.objective: LO: I can multiply whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 by shifting place value.

content.text: Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one column LEFT. The digits stay the same; their place value changes.
Common error: ‘just add a zero.’ That works only for whole numbers. For decimals, you must shift digits (3.4 × 10 = 34, not 3.40).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiplying by 10 = shift digits 1 left. By 100 = shift 2 left. By 1000 = shift 3 left. The decimal point appears to move RIGHT.
key_idea.caption: Decimal point moves 2 places right

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – whole × 10
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 47 × 10
modelled_examples.explanation: Add a zero in the units column to mark the new place.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – whole × 100
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 23 × 100
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiplying by 100 = multiplying by 10 twice.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – decimal × 10
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 3.6 × 10
modelled_examples.explanation: The 6 moves from tenths to ones.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – decimal × 1000
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 0.045 × 1000
modelled_examples.explanation: Decimal point moves 3 places right.

problems.text: A box of pencils contains 100 pencils. A school orders 34 boxes. How many pencils in total? Use ×100 to find the answer.
A water bottle holds 0.75 litres. A factory fills 1000 bottles an hour. How many litres of water are used per hour? Show your working.

100-6-7-9-11-12-times-tables.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(6, 7, 9, 11 AND 12 TIMES TABLES)
100-6-7-9-11-12-times-tables.objective: LO: I can recall the harder times tables (6, 7, 9, 11, 12) and use them to solve problems.

content.text: The 9 times table trick: the digits of every multiple of 9 add to 9 (e.g. 36 → 3+6 = 9). Or use 10×n then subtract n: 9×7 = 70 − 7 = 63.
11 times table trick: for 1−9, just repeat the digit (4×11 = 44, 7×11 = 77).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Use friendly facts to bridge to harder ones. e.g. 7×6 = (7×5) + 7 = 35 + 7 = 42.
key_idea.caption: ×10 then subtract

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – 9 times table trick
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 9 × 6
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiples of 9 are always one less than 10×n.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – 7 times table
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 7 × 8
modelled_examples.explanation: Use the square fact 7×7=49 as a stepping stone.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – 12 times table
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 12 × 8
modelled_examples.explanation: Split 12 into 10 + 2 and multiply each separately.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – 11 times table
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 11 × 7
modelled_examples.explanation: 11 × 12 breaks the rule: it's 132, not 1212.

practice.instruction: Recall as fast as you can.

practice.heading: 9 times table
practice.instruction: Use the ×10−n trick if you need to.

practice.heading: 11 times table

A baker makes trays of 12 buns. She bakes for 6 hours and produces 1 tray every 30 minutes. How many buns does she make in total?

102-short-division.title:
DIVISION,
(SHORT DIVISION)
102-short-division.objective: LO: I can use short division (bus-stop) to divide by a single-digit number.

content.text: Short division is a quick written method for dividing by a SINGLE-digit number. We carry remainders mentally.
When to use: dividing by 2-9. For 10+, use long division.

examples.expr: Skip a digit if too small

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Divide each digit left-to-right. If a digit is too small, carry to the next as a remainder.
key_idea.caption: Left to right; carry small remainders

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – no remainder
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 84 ÷ 4
modelled_examples.explanation: Check: 21 × 4 = 84 ✓

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – with carry
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 75 ÷ 3
modelled_examples.explanation: The remainder ‘1’ from 7÷3 joins the next digit 5 to make 15.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – with remainder
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 85 ÷ 4
modelled_examples.explanation: Final remainder is left over because no more digits to bring down.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – writing zero
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 612 ÷ 6
modelled_examples.explanation: When a digit doesn't divide, write 0 in the answer.

practice.heading: With carry
practice.instruction: Carry small remainders to the next digit.

practice.heading: Writing zero in answer
practice.instruction: If a digit doesn't divide, write 0 in the answer.

items.statement: Carry remainders to the next digit on the RIGHT
Short division works for any divisor
Always check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend

problems.text: 936 sweets are shared equally between 8 children. How many sweets each? Are any left over? Show your short division.
A school orders 525 textbooks packed in boxes of 7. How many full boxes? Now imagine 530 books. How many full boxes and how many spare?

103-short-multiplication.title:
MULTIPLICATION,
(SHORT MULTIPLICATION)
103-short-multiplication.objective: LO: I can multiply a multi-digit number by a single digit using short multiplication.

content.text: Short multiplication is the column method for multi-digit × SINGLE-digit. Multiply each digit, carry tens to the next column.
When to use: multiplying by 2-9. For 10+, use long multiplication.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply each digit (right to left). If the result is 10+, write the units and CARRY the tens to the next column.
key_idea.caption: 8×7=56, write 6 carry 5; then 8×4+5=37

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – no carry
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 32 × 3
modelled_examples.explanation: No carrying needed because each multiplication is < 10.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – single carry
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 47 × 8
modelled_examples.explanation: Always work right to left, carrying any tens.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – 3-digit number
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 234 × 6
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiple carries: each one adds to the next column.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – with zero
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 305 × 7
modelled_examples.explanation: Zeros multiply to give 0 — but carries still apply.

practice.heading: With carrying
practice.instruction: Carry the tens to the next column.

practice.heading: With zero in number
practice.instruction: Don't forget: 0 × n = 0, plus any carry.

items.statement: Carries are added to the NEXT column's product
Short multiplication only works for single-digit multipliers

problems.text: A book has 247 pages. A library has 9 copies. How many pages in total across all copies? Use short multiplication.
A factory makes 1234 widgets a day, 7 days a week. How many widgets per week? How many in 4 weeks? Show your working clearly.

104-compound-interest-and-depreciation.title:
PERCENTAGES,
(COMPOUND INTEREST AND DEPRECIATION)
104-compound-interest-and-depreciation.objective: LO: I can calculate compound interest and depreciation using repeated percentage change.

content.text: Compound interest is earned on the original amount AND on previous interest. Depreciation is when a value decreases by a fixed percentage each year.
Formula: Final value = Original × (multiplier)<sup>n</sup>, where n is the number of years.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Use the multiplier raised to the power of years. Growth: 1 + r. Depreciation: 1 - r.
key_idea.caption: P = principal, r = rate as decimal, n = years

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – compound interest
modelled_examples.question: £2000 is invested at 4% compound interest for 3 years. Find the final amount.
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply by the growth multiplier for each year.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – finding interest earned
modelled_examples.question: £5000 at 3% compound interest for 2 years. How much interest is earned?
modelled_examples.explanation: Subtract the original to find just the interest.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – depreciation
modelled_examples.question: A car worth £12000 depreciates by 15% per year. Find its value after 4 years.
modelled_examples.explanation: Depreciation uses a multiplier less than 1.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – finding the rate
modelled_examples.question: A painting increases from £500 to £605 in 2 years compound. Find the annual rate.
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide by the original, then take the nth root.

practice.heading: Interest earned
practice.instruction: Find the interest earned (final amount minus principal).

practice.heading: Comparing simple and compound
practice.instruction: Calculate both simple and compound interest, then find the difference.

House worth £200000 increases 6% per year for 3 years. New value?

items.statement: Compound interest grows faster than simple interest
5% compound interest for 3 years is 15% total increase
Depreciation of 20% per year uses multiplier 0.8
After 100% depreciation the item is worthless
The compound interest formula is A = P(1 + r)^n

problems.text: Priya invests £5000 at 3.5% compound interest. After how many complete years will her investment first exceed £6000? Show your working.

105-percentage-increase-and-decrease.title:
PERCENTAGES,
(PERCENTAGE INCREASE AND DECREASE)
105-percentage-increase-and-decrease.objective: LO: I can increase or decrease an amount by a given percentage using a multiplier.

content.text: A percentage increase makes an amount larger. A percentage decrease makes it smaller. Use a single multiplier for efficiency.
Multiplier method: Increase by 15% means × 1.15. Decrease by 15% means × 0.85.

examples.expr: Increase by 25% then decrease by 25% = original

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: To increase, add the percentage to 100% to get the multiplier. To decrease, subtract from 100%.
key_idea.caption: Increase: 1 + &frac{%}{100}. Decrease: 1 - &frac{%}{100}

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – percentage increase
modelled_examples.question: Increase £240 by 15%
modelled_examples.explanation: The multiplier 1.15 means 100% + 15% = 115% of original.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – percentage decrease
modelled_examples.question: Decrease £350 by 20%
modelled_examples.explanation: 0.80 means keeping 80% (removing 20%).

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – VAT calculation
modelled_examples.question: A TV costs £450 before VAT at 20%. Find the price including VAT.
modelled_examples.explanation: VAT is a percentage increase on the original price.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – reverse percentage
modelled_examples.question: After a 20% increase, a price is £360. Find the original.
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide by the multiplier to reverse a percentage change.

practice.instruction: Increase each amount by the given percentage.

practice.heading: Percentage decreases
practice.instruction: Decrease each amount by the given percentage.

practice.instruction: Write the single multiplier for each change.

106-percentage-of-an-amount.title:
PERCENTAGES,
(PERCENTAGE OF AN AMOUNT)
106-percentage-of-an-amount.objective: LO: I can calculate a percentage of an amount using mental and written methods.

key_terms.title: Finding a percentage of an amount

content.text: To find a percentage of an amount, divide by 100 to find 1%, then multiply by the percentage needed. Or use the multiplier method.
Multiplier: 35% of 80 = 0.35 × 80 = 28. The percentage as a decimal IS the multiplier.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Percentage means per hundred. Divide by 100 to find 1%, then scale up.
key_idea.caption: Convert percentage to decimal, then multiply

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – using 10%
modelled_examples.question: Find 30% of 90
modelled_examples.explanation: Find 10% first, then multiply by 3 for 30%.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – using the multiplier
modelled_examples.question: Find 45% of 200
modelled_examples.explanation: The multiplier method works for any percentage.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – building percentages
modelled_examples.question: Find 17.5% of 60
modelled_examples.explanation: Break awkward percentages into easier parts.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – percentage of money
modelled_examples.question: Find 12% of £350
modelled_examples.explanation: Find 1% by dividing by 100, then multiply up.

107-finding-any-percentage-of-an-amount.title:
PERCENTAGES OF AMOUNTS,
(FINDING ANY PERCENTAGE OF AN AMOUNT)
107-finding-any-percentage-of-an-amount.objective: LO: I can find any percentage of an amount using a calculator or written method.

content.text: To find any percentage of an amount, write the percentage as a decimal or fraction and multiply. This method works for whole and decimal percentages.
Method: Convert the percentage to a decimal (divide by 100), then multiply by the amount.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Any percentage can be found by converting to a decimal and multiplying.
key_idea.caption: Works for any P, including decimals and values over 100

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – whole number percentage
modelled_examples.question: Find 37% of 250
modelled_examples.explanation: Divide the percentage by 100 to get the decimal multiplier.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – decimal percentage
modelled_examples.question: Find 3.5% of 600
modelled_examples.explanation: Decimal percentages work the same way.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – percentage over 100

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – real-world context

modelled_examples.explanation: Same decimal multiplier method applied to money.

108-percentage-increase-and-decrease-pri.title:
PERCENTAGES OF AMOUNTS,
(PERCENTAGE INCREASE AND DECREASE)
108-percentage-increase-and-decrease-pri.objective: LO: I can find a percentage increase or decrease and express a change as a percentage.

content.text: A percentage change tells you how much something has gone up or down compared to the original amount, expressed as a percentage.
Formula: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100%

examples.expr: Always divide by the ORIGINAL amount

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Percentage change = (difference ÷ original) × 100. Always divide by the ORIGINAL value.
key_idea.caption: Divide by the starting value, not the new value

132-estimating-calculations.title:
PLACE VALUE AND ORDERING INTEGERS,
(ESTIMATING CALCULATIONS)
132-estimating-calculations.objective: LO: I can estimate answers to calculations by rounding numbers to one significant figure.

content.text: To estimate a calculation, round each number to one significant figure (1 s.f.) first, then perform the calculation with the rounded values.
Why estimate? Estimating checks your answer is sensible and helps spot errors.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Round every number to 1 significant figure, then calculate. The symbol ≈ means approximately equal to.
key_idea.caption: Round each value to 1 s.f. before calculating

133-ordering-positive-and-negative-integ.title:
PLACE VALUE AND ORDERING INTEGERS,
(ORDERING POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE INTEGERS)
133-ordering-positive-and-negative-integ.objective: LO: I can order and compare positive and negative integers using a number line.

content.text: Integers are whole numbers including negatives, zero, and positives. On a number line, numbers increase from left to right.
Key rule: A negative number is always less than a positive number. The further left on the number line, the smaller the value.

examples.expr: 0 is greater than any negative number

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Picture a number line: numbers to the right are always bigger. Negative numbers are to the left of zero.
key_idea.caption: Left = smaller, Right = bigger

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – ordering negatives
modelled_examples.question: Put these in order from smallest to largest: -3, 5, -7, 2, -1
modelled_examples.explanation: The more negative a number, the smaller it is.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – comparing two integers
modelled_examples.question: Which is greater: -4 or -9?
steps: On the number line, -4 is to the right of -9
modelled_examples.explanation: Closer to zero means bigger for negative numbers.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – using inequality symbols
modelled_examples.question: Insert < or >: -6 ___ -2
steps: On the number line, -6 is to the left of -2
modelled_examples.explanation: The open end of < points to the bigger number.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – temperature context
modelled_examples.question: Order these temperatures from coldest to warmest: 3°C, -5°C, -1°C, 8°C, -8°C

134-reading-and-writing-large-integers.title:
PLACE VALUE AND ORDERING INTEGERS,
(READING AND WRITING LARGE INTEGERS)
134-reading-and-writing-large-integers.objective: LO: I can read, write and compare large integers up to millions using place value.

content.text: Place value tells us the value of each digit based on its position. Large numbers use thousands, millions, and billions columns.
Commas: We use commas (or spaces) to separate groups of three digits from the right, making large numbers easier to read.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Use place value columns: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands, millions.
key_idea.caption: 2 millions, 456 thousands, 789 ones

steps: Four million two hundred and fifty thousand
modelled_examples.answer: = Four million two hundred and fifty thousand
modelled_examples.explanation: Read from left to right using place value.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – writing in figures

steps: Seven hundred and thirty-two thousand = 732 thousand
modelled_examples.explanation: Match each word to its place value position.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – identifying digit value
modelled_examples.question: What is the value of the 6 in 3,604,500?
steps: Position: millions column has 3, hundred-thousands has 6
The 6 is in the hundred-thousands column
modelled_examples.explanation: The position of the digit determines its value.

modelled_examples.question: Which is larger: 2,450,000 or 2,540,000?

135-rounding-to-significant-figures.title:
PLACE VALUE AND ORDERING INTEGERS,
(ROUNDING TO SIGNIFICANT FIGURES)
135-rounding-to-significant-figures.objective: LO: I can round numbers to a given number of significant figures.

content.text: Significant figures (s.f.) are counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros are not significant but trailing zeros after a decimal point are.
Rule: Find the digit at the required position, look at the next digit. If it is 5 or more, round up.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Count significant figures from the first non-zero digit. Round using normal rounding rules.
key_idea.caption: Leading zeros are placeholders, not significant

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – rounding whole numbers
modelled_examples.question: Round 5738 to 2 significant figures.
steps: Next digit is 3 (< 5), so round down
modelled_examples.explanation: Fill remaining places with zeros to keep the number the right size.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – rounding decimals
modelled_examples.question: Round 0.04562 to 2 significant figures.
steps: Skip leading zeros: first s.f. is 4, second is 5
Next digit is 6 (≥ 5), so round up
modelled_examples.explanation: Leading zeros are not counted as significant.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – rounding to 3 s.f.
modelled_examples.question: Round 24,850 to 3 significant figures.
steps: Next digit is 5 (≥ 5), so round up
modelled_examples.explanation: The 8 becomes 9 because the next digit is 5.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – rounding to 1 s.f.
modelled_examples.question: Round 0.000394 to 1 significant figure.
steps: Skip leading zeros: first s.f. is 3

modelled_examples.explanation: Only one non-zero digit remains in the answer.

136-basic-probability-single-events.title:
PROBABILITY,
(BASIC PROBABILITY SINGLE EVENTS)
136-basic-probability-single-events.objective: LO: I can calculate the probability of a single event using fractions.

content.text: Probability measures how likely something is to happen, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It equals favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
Key rule: P(event) = number of ways the event can happen ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes.

examples.expr: P(heads) = &frac{1}{3} because heads, tails, or edge
P(6 on a die) = &frac{1}{3} because even or odd or 6

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Probability = favourable outcomes divided by total equally likely outcomes.
key_idea.caption: Always a value between 0 and 1

modelled_examples.explanation: Count the favourable outcomes and divide by total.

137-conditional-probability-and-venn-dia.title:
PROBABILITY,

137-conditional-probability-and-venn-dia.objective: LO: I can use Venn diagrams to find probabilities including conditional probability.

content.text: Conditional probability is the probability of an event given that another event has already occurred. Venn diagrams help us visualise overlapping groups.
Notation: P(A|B) means the probability of A given B. P(A|B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).

examples.expr: A Venn diagram shows overlapping sets

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: In a Venn diagram, the overlap shows items in BOTH sets. Conditional probability restricts to a subset.
key_idea.caption: Given B, only look at members of B

138-mutually-exclusive-events.title:

138-mutually-exclusive-events.objective: LO: I can identify mutually exclusive events and use the addition rule for probability.

content.text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time. If one occurs, the other cannot occur.
Addition rule: If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

examples.expr: Rolling a 3 and rolling a 5 on one die: mutually exclusive
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when mutually exclusive
All probabilities in a sample space sum to 1
Drawing a red card and a king are mutually exclusive
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) always

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Mutually exclusive events have no overlap: P(A and B) = 0. So P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
key_idea.caption: Only when A and B cannot happen together

content.text: A quadratic sequence has a constant second difference. The nth term has the form an² + bn + c.
Strategy: Find first differences, then second differences. If the second difference is constant (= 2a), the sequence is quadratic. Then find a, b, c.

161-solving-by-elimination.title:

161-solving-by-elimination.objective: LO: I can solve simultaneous linear equations by adding or subtracting to eliminate a variable.

content.text: The elimination method removes one variable by adding or subtracting the equations. We make the coefficients of one variable equal (by multiplying), then add or subtract.
Strategy: Same signs = subtract. Different signs = add. Then solve for the remaining variable and substitute back.

content.text: The substitution method involves rearranging one equation to make a variable the subject, then replacing that variable in the other equation.

172-gradient-and-y-intercept.objective: LO: I can calculate the gradient of a line and identify the y-intercept from a graph or coordinates.

content.text: The gradient measures how steep a line is: rise ÷ run. A positive gradient slopes upward; a negative gradient slopes downward.
Y-intercept: The point where the line crosses the y-axis (where x = 0). Written as (0, c).

examples.desc: change in y over change in x

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Gradient = change in y divided by change in x. Pick any two points on the line.
key_idea.caption: Rise over run

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – from two points
modelled_examples.question: Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (5, 9).
modelled_examples.explanation: Subtract y-values for rise, x-values for run.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – negative gradient
modelled_examples.question: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 7) and (4, 1).
modelled_examples.explanation: A negative answer means the line slopes downward.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – from a graph
modelled_examples.question: A line passes through (0, 4) and (3, 4). Find the gradient.
modelled_examples.explanation: A horizontal line has zero gradient.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – finding the y-intercept
modelled_examples.question: A line has gradient 3 and passes through (2, 8). Find the y-intercept.
modelled_examples.explanation: Substitute a known point into y = mx + c to find c.

practice.instruction: Find the gradient and state whether it slopes up or down.

practice.heading: Fractional gradients
practice.instruction: Calculate the gradient. Leave as a fraction if needed.

practice.instruction: Find the y-intercept using y = mx + c.

A vertical line has gradient zero

173-parallel-and-perpendicular-lines.title:
STRAIGHT-LINE GRAPHS,
(PARALLEL AND PERPENDICULAR LINES)
173-parallel-and-perpendicular-lines.objective: LO: I can identify and find equations of parallel and perpendicular lines.

content.text: Parallel lines have the same gradient (m₁ = m₂). Perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to give -1.
Key rule: If one line has gradient m, a perpendicular line has gradient -&frac{1}{m} (the negative reciprocal).

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Parallel: same gradient. Perpendicular: gradients multiply to -1.
key_idea.caption: Negative reciprocal for perpendicular lines

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – identifying parallel lines
modelled_examples.question: Are y = 3x + 5 and y = 3x - 2 parallel?
steps: Same gradient, so they are parallel
modelled_examples.explanation: Parallel lines have equal gradients but different y-intercepts.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – perpendicular gradient
modelled_examples.question: Find the gradient perpendicular to y = 4x + 1.
modelled_examples.explanation: Flip the fraction and change the sign.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – equation of parallel line
modelled_examples.question: Find the line parallel to y = 2x + 3 through (1, 5).
modelled_examples.explanation: Use the same gradient and find c from the given point.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – equation of perpendicular line
modelled_examples.question: Find the line perpendicular to y = 3x - 1 through (6, 2).
modelled_examples.explanation: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and substitute the point.

practice.instruction: State whether each pair is parallel, perpendicular, or neither.

practice.heading: Equations of parallel lines
practice.instruction: Find the equation of the parallel line through the given point.

practice.heading: Equations of perpendicular lines
practice.instruction: Find the equation of the perpendicular line through the given point.

Line perpendicular to y = 5x at (0, 2). Equation?

items.statement: Parallel lines have the same gradient

174-plotting-straight-line-graphs.title:
STRAIGHT-LINE GRAPHS,
(PLOTTING STRAIGHT-LINE GRAPHS)
174-plotting-straight-line-graphs.objective: LO: I can plot straight-line graphs by generating a table of values and drawing the line.

content.text: To plot a straight line, substitute values of x into the equation to find corresponding y-values. Plot these coordinate pairs and join with a ruler.
Tip: You only need two points to draw a line, but use three to check for errors.

examples.expr: y = 2x + 1: when x = 0, y = 1; when x = 2, y = 5
Use x = 0, 1, 2, 3 to make a table of values
Three collinear points confirms the line
Only need one point to draw a line

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Substitute at least three x-values into the equation. Plot the (x, y) pairs and join with a straight line.
key_idea.equation: x = 0 ⇒ y = c, x = 1 ⇒ y = m + c
key_idea.caption: Start with x = 0 to find the y-intercept

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – table of values
modelled_examples.question: Complete a table for y = 3x - 1 with x = 0, 1, 2, 3.
modelled_examples.explanation: Substitute each x-value into the equation.

modelled_examples.question: Plot y = 2x - 4 using x and y intercepts.
modelled_examples.explanation: Intercepts give two quick points without a full table.

modelled_examples.question: Plot y = -x + 3 for x = 0 to 4.
modelled_examples.explanation: A negative gradient makes the line slope down from left to right.

modelled_examples.question: Plot y = &frac{1}{2}x + 1 for x = 0, 2, 4, 6.
steps: Gentle slope, rising by 1 for every 2 across
modelled_examples.explanation: Choose even x-values to avoid fractions in the y-coordinates.

175-adding-and-subtracting-surds.title:
SURDS,
(ADDING AND SUBTRACTING SURDS)
175-adding-and-subtracting-surds.objective: LO: I can add and subtract surds by collecting like surd terms.

content.text: A surd is an irrational root such as √2 or √5. We can only add or subtract surds that have the same number under the root sign (like terms).
Simplify first: Sometimes surds need to be simplified before they can be combined. For example, √8 = 2√2.

examples.desc: cannot add unlike surds under one root

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Only like surds (same radicand) can be added or subtracted. Simplify surds first to reveal like terms.
key_idea.caption: Collect like surd terms

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – like surds
modelled_examples.question: Simplify 4√3 + 7√3.
modelled_examples.explanation: Treat surds like algebra: add the coefficients of like terms.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – subtraction
modelled_examples.question: Simplify 9√2 - 5√2.
modelled_examples.explanation: Same process for subtraction.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – simplify first
modelled_examples.question: Simplify √18 + √2.
modelled_examples.explanation: Simplify surds before combining.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – mixed expression
modelled_examples.question: Simplify √50 - √8 + √32.
modelled_examples.explanation: Simplify each surd, then combine like terms.

practice.heading: Simplify first, then combine
practice.instruction: Simplify each surd, then add or subtract.

problems.text: Simplify √200 + √50 - √72 + √18. Express your answer in the form a√2 where a is an integer.
The sides of a triangle are √48 cm, √27 cm, and √75 cm. Find the perimeter in simplified surd form. If the perimeter is doubled, write the new perimeter.

176-multiplying-and-dividing-surds.title:
SURDS,
(MULTIPLYING AND DIVIDING SURDS)
176-multiplying-and-dividing-surds.objective: LO: I can multiply and divide surds using the rules of surds.

content.text: To multiply surds: √a × √b = √(ab). To divide surds: √a ÷ √b = √(a/b).
Key fact: √a × √a = a. Simplify the result where possible.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply or divide the numbers under the root sign. Multiply coefficients separately.
key_idea.caption: Same rule works for division: √a ÷ √b = √(a ÷ b)

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – multiplying simple surds
modelled_examples.question: Calculate √3 × √7.
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply the radicands together.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – with coefficients
modelled_examples.question: Calculate 3√2 × 4√5.
modelled_examples.explanation: Coefficients multiply separately from the surds.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – simplifying the product
modelled_examples.question: Calculate √6 × √8.
modelled_examples.explanation: Always check if the product simplifies.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – dividing surds
modelled_examples.question: Calculate √72 ÷ √2.
modelled_examples.explanation: When dividing, divide the numbers under the root.

problems.text: Show that (√5 + √3)(√5 - √3) = 2. Use this result to explain why the product of conjugate surds is always rational.
A rectangle has area 12√6 cm² and width 2√3 cm. Find the length in simplified surd form. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

177-rationalising-the-denominator.title:
SURDS,
(RATIONALISING THE DENOMINATOR)
177-rationalising-the-denominator.objective: LO: I can rationalise the denominator of a fraction containing surds.

content.text: Rationalising means removing the surd from the denominator. Multiply top and bottom by the surd in the denominator (or its conjugate).
Conjugate: For denominators like a + √b, multiply by a - √b (the conjugate) to eliminate the surd.

examples.desc: must multiply both top and bottom

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by the surd (or conjugate) to make the denominator rational.
key_idea.caption: Since √b × √b = b

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – simple rationalisation
modelled_examples.question: Rationalise &frac{1}{√5}.
modelled_examples.explanation: Multiply by √5 over √5 (which equals 1).

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – with a coefficient
modelled_examples.question: Rationalise &frac{6}{√3}.
modelled_examples.explanation: After rationalising, simplify the fraction.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – using the conjugate
modelled_examples.question: Rationalise &frac{3}{2 + √5}.
modelled_examples.explanation: The denominator becomes (a+b)(a-b) = a² - b².

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – harder conjugate
modelled_examples.question: Rationalise &frac{4}{√7 - √3}.
modelled_examples.explanation: Difference of two surds: use the sum as conjugate.

items.statement: To rationalise &frac{1}{√3}, multiply top and bottom by √3

problems.text: Show that &frac{1}{√2 + 1} + &frac{1}{√3 + √2} + &frac{1}{√4 + √3} = 1 by rationalising each fraction.
Rationalise &frac{5 + √3}{2 - √3} and express in the form a + b√3 where a and b are integers.

178-simplifying-surds.title:
SURDS,
(SIMPLIFYING SURDS)
178-simplifying-surds.objective: LO: I can simplify surds by finding the largest square factor.

content.text: To simplify a surd, find the largest perfect square factor of the number under the root sign and take its square root outside.
Method: √n = √(a² × b) = a√b. Choose the largest perfect square factor for efficiency.

examples.desc: neither factor is a perfect square

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Find the largest perfect square that divides the number. Take its root outside the radical.
key_idea.equation: √n = a√b where n = a² × b
key_idea.caption: b should have no perfect square factors left

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – basic simplification
modelled_examples.question: Simplify √20.
modelled_examples.explanation: 4 is the largest perfect square that divides 20.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – larger number
modelled_examples.question: Simplify √45.
modelled_examples.explanation: 9 is the largest perfect square that divides 45.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – with coefficient
modelled_examples.question: Simplify 3√28.
modelled_examples.explanation: Simplify the surd first, then multiply by the outer coefficient.

items.statement: A surd is fully simplified when no perfect square divides the radicand

179-enlargement.title:
TRANSFORMATIONS,
(ENLARGEMENT)
179-enlargement.objective: LO: I can enlarge a shape by a given scale factor from a centre of enlargement.

content.text: An enlargement changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a fixed point called the centre of enlargement.
Key fact: Scale factor > 1 makes the shape bigger. Scale factor between 0 and 1 makes it smaller. Negative scale factor also inverts the image.

examples.expr: SF 2 from centre: all distances from centre doubled
SF &frac{1}{2}: image is half the size
SF -1: image inverted through the centre

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply the distance from the centre to each vertex by the scale factor to find the image vertices.
key_idea.equation: image distance = SF × object distance from centre
key_idea.caption: Measure distances from the centre of enlargement

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – scale factor 2 from origin
modelled_examples.question: Enlarge triangle (1,1), (3,1), (1,3) by SF 2 from (0,0).
modelled_examples.explanation: From the origin, just multiply all coordinates by the SF.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – scale factor 3 from a point
modelled_examples.question: Enlarge point (2,1) by SF 3 from centre (1,0).
modelled_examples.explanation: Find the vector from centre to point, multiply by SF, add back to centre.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – fractional scale factor
modelled_examples.question: Enlarge (6,4) by SF &frac{1}{2} from centre (0,0).
modelled_examples.explanation: Fractional scale factors reduce the shape.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – negative scale factor
modelled_examples.question: Enlarge (3,1) by SF -2 from centre (1,1).
modelled_examples.explanation: Negative SF puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.

180-reflection.title:
TRANSFORMATIONS,
(REFLECTION)
180-reflection.objective: LO: I can reflect shapes in mirror lines including the axes and the lines y = x and y = -x.

content.text: A reflection flips a shape across a mirror line. Each point and its image are the same distance from the mirror line.
Common mirror lines: x-axis (y = 0), y-axis (x = 0), y = x (diagonal), y = -x, and vertical/horizontal lines like x = 2.

examples.expr: Reflection changes the size of the shape

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Each point is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line as its image, on the opposite side.
key_idea.equation: (a, b) in y-axis → (-a, b)
key_idea.caption: Reflecting in the y-axis negates the x-coordinate

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – reflection in y-axis
modelled_examples.question: Reflect (4, 3) in the y-axis.
modelled_examples.explanation: Reflection in y-axis: (x, y) becomes (-x, y).

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – reflection in x-axis
modelled_examples.question: Reflect (-2, 5) in the x-axis.
modelled_examples.explanation: Reflection in x-axis: (x, y) becomes (x, -y).

steps: Image is 3 to the left of x = 2

181-rotation.title:
TRANSFORMATIONS,
(ROTATION)
181-rotation.objective: LO: I can rotate shapes about a given centre by 90, 180, or 270 degrees.

content.text: A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point called the centre of rotation. You need to know the centre, angle, and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise).
Key rules: 90° clockwise: (x,y)→(y,-x). 90° anticlockwise: (x,y)→(-y,x). 180°: (x,y)→(-x,-y) about the origin.

examples.expr: 90° clockwise is the same as 90° anticlockwise
Rotation changes the size of the shape

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: To describe a rotation, state: centre, angle, and direction. The shape does not change size.
key_idea.equation: 90° CW about O: (x, y) → (y, -x)
key_idea.caption: 180°: (x, y) → (-x, -y)

modelled_examples.explanation: Negate both coordinates.

modelled_examples.explanation: Translate to origin, rotate, translate back.

182-translation.title:
TRANSFORMATIONS,
(TRANSLATION)
182-translation.objective: LO: I can translate shapes using a column vector.

content.text: A translation slides a shape without rotating or flipping it. It is described by a column vector that shows the horizontal and vertical movement.
Column vector: The top number is the horizontal shift (positive = right) and the bottom number is the vertical shift (positive = up).

examples.desc: top is horizontal, bottom is vertical

183-exact-trigonometric-values.title:
TRIGONOMETRY,
(EXACT TRIGONOMETRIC VALUES)
183-exact-trigonometric-values.objective: LO: I can recall and use exact values of sin, cos, and tan for 0, 30, 45, 60, and 90 degrees.

content.text: The exact values of sin, cos, and tan at key angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) can be expressed as surds or fractions without a calculator.
Key facts: sin 30° = &frac{1}{2}, cos 60° = &frac{1}{2}, tan 45° = 1. These come from equilateral triangles and isosceles right-angled triangles.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Learn the exact values from the 30-60-90 triangle (sides 1, √3, 2) and the 45-45-90 triangle (sides 1, 1, √2).
key_idea.caption: Derived from half an equilateral triangle

modelled_examples.explanation: Both sin and cos of 45° are equal.

modelled_examples.explanation: tan = opposite/adjacent = 1/√3.

184-soh-cah-toa-finding-angles.title:
TRIGONOMETRY,
(SOH CAH TOA FINDING ANGLES)
184-soh-cah-toa-finding-angles.objective: LO: I can use inverse trigonometric functions to find unknown angles in right-angled triangles.

content.text: To find an unknown angle, use the inverse trig functions: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, or tan⁻¹. Choose which ratio to use based on which two sides are known.
SOH CAH TOA: Sin = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cos = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tan = Opposite/Adjacent.

examples.expr: Use sin when you have adjacent and hypotenuse

key_idea.title: Key idea

content.text: To find an unknown side, label the sides (O, A, H) relative to the given angle, then use the appropriate ratio: SOH, CAH, or TOA.

186-sine-and-cosine-rules.title:
TRIGONOMETRY,
(SINE AND COSINE RULES)
186-sine-and-cosine-rules.objective: LO: I can apply the sine rule and cosine rule to find unknown sides and angles in non-right-angled triangles.

content.text: The sine rule is used when you have a side and its opposite angle: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. The cosine rule is used when you know two sides and the included angle (or all three sides).
Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A. To find an angle: cos A = (b² + c² - a²) ÷ 2bc.

VECTORS,
(ADDING AND SUBTRACTING VECTORS)
187-adding-and-subtracting-vectors.objective: LO: I can add and subtract column vectors and represent the results on a grid.

content.text: A vector has magnitude and direction, written as a column vector. To add vectors, add the corresponding components. To subtract, subtract components.
Geometrically: Adding vectors places them end to end (triangle rule). The resultant goes from the start of the first to the end of the last.

188-multiplying-vectors-by-a-scalar.title:
VECTORS,
(MULTIPLYING VECTORS BY A SCALAR)
188-multiplying-vectors-by-a-scalar.objective: LO: I can multiply a vector by a scalar and understand its geometric effect.

content.text: Multiplying a vector by a scalar (number) multiplies each component by that number. This scales the vector: changing its magnitude but not its direction (unless negative).
Key fact: A negative scalar reverses the direction. Vectors that are scalar multiples of each other are parallel.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Multiply each component by the scalar. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other.

189-vector-geometry-proofs.title:
VECTORS,
(VECTOR GEOMETRY PROOFS)
189-vector-geometry-proofs.objective: LO: I can use vectors to prove geometric results involving midpoints, parallel lines, and collinear points.

content.text: In vector geometry, we express journeys around a shape in terms of vectors a and b. If two vectors are parallel (scalar multiples), the lines are parallel.
Key strategies: To prove collinearity, show one vector is a scalar multiple of another AND they share a common point. The midpoint of AB has position vector &frac{1}{2}(a + b).

If PQ = kRS, then PQ is parallel to RS

VECTORS,
(WRITING AND REPRESENTING VECTORS)
190-writing-and-representing-vectors.objective: LO: I can write vectors using column notation and represent them on a grid.

content.text: A vector describes a movement with both magnitude (size) and direction. We write column vectors as (x, y) where x is the horizontal movement and y is the vertical movement.
Convention: Positive x means right, negative x means left. Positive y means up, negative y means down. Vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction.

191-surface-area-of-cylinders-and-sphere.title:
VOLUME AND SURFACE AREA,
(SURFACE AREA OF CYLINDERS AND SPHERES)
191-surface-area-of-cylinders-and-sphere.objective: LO: I can calculate the surface area of cylinders and spheres using formulae.

key_terms.title: Surface area of cylinders and spheres

content.text: The surface area of a 3D shape is the total area of all its faces. A cylinder has two circular ends and a curved surface that unfolds into a rectangle. A sphere has a single curved surface.
Formulae: Cylinder SA = 2πr² + 2πrh. Sphere SA = 4πr². Always include units² in your answer.

examples.desc: four times the area of a great circle

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Surface area is the total area covering the outside of a 3D shape. Use the correct formula for each shape.
key_idea.caption: Two circular ends plus the curved surface area

VOLUME AND SURFACE AREA,

192-surface-area-of-prisms.objective: LO: I can calculate the surface area of prisms by finding the area of each face.

content.text: A prism is a 3D shape with a uniform cross-section. Its surface area is the sum of the areas of all its faces: two identical end faces plus the rectangular side faces.
Method: Find the area of the cross-section (end face), double it for both ends, then add the areas of each rectangular side. SA = 2 × (area of cross-section) + (perimeter of cross-section) × length.

key_terms.title: Volume of pyramids, cones and spheres

content.text: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at an apex. A cone is a circular pyramid. Their volumes are one-third of the corresponding prism or cylinder.
Key formulae: Pyramid: V = &frac{1}{3} × base area × height. Cone: V = &frac{1}{3}πr²h. Sphere: V = &frac{4}{3}πr³.

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Pyramids and cones have volume equal to one-third of the corresponding prism or cylinder. A sphere uses its own formula with r cubed.
